summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, so county social workers were not liable for failing to remove a child they knew was being abused.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that a screen-out or closed investigation generally creates no federal constitutional liability.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.holding: In a wrongful-death action arising from a fatal child abuse case, the court held that the reporting statute's immunity under Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 37-1-410(a) protects only persons who actually make a report of harm, and that the physician who did not report was not immune.
key_cases.relevance: Illustrates the liability exposure created when suspected abuse is not reported or is screened out.
key_cases.quote: immunity under Tennessee Code Annotated section 37-1-410(a) is afforded only to those who actually report harm

key_cases.case_name: Fitzpatrick v. Tennessee Department of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Reviewing DCS's classification of foster parents as indicated perpetrators of neglect, the court held they received the fundamentally fair procedures due process requires through the file review and contested administrative hearing, affirmed the lack-of-supervision indication, and remanded on attorney's fees for the reversed environmental-neglect indication.
key_cases.relevance: Explains the unfounded-versus-indicated determination DCS must make within sixty days.
key_cases.quote: Procedural due process requires a government entity to employ fundamentally fair procedures whenever it acts to deprive a person of a right to or interest in life, liberty, or property.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal of the parents' section 1983 claims, holding that a child-abuse investigation standing alone, without removal or another deprivation of custody or control, does not infringe the constitutional right to familial association.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why a screened-out or closed investigation ordinarily gives a family no federal constitutional claim.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the right to familial association is not implicated merely by governmental investigation into allegations of child abuse.
